S01.headline: Some days are harder than others. It helps to know which.
S01.sub: SteadyAir keeps a short, honest record of how your breathing has been — the kind of thing that is very hard to remember accurately in a ten-minute appointment, and very easy to write down in twenty seconds a day.

blocks.title: Twenty seconds, most days
blocks.body: A number out of ten and how many times you reached for your reliever. That is the whole of it.

blocks.title: It routes, it doesn't judge
blocks.body: When your own numbers start moving, SteadyAir says so and points you at your nurse. It will never tell you what to take.

blocks.title: Nothing leaves your phone on its own
blocks.body: Not to your clinic, not to your family. You see the exact contents first, or it doesn't go.

S01.footer: Education and self-management support. Not a diagnosis or treatment, and not a substitute for advice from a qualified health professional.

S02.title: What it does
S02.headline: Four moments this is built for.
S02.sub: Not four features. Four points where living with a long-term chest condition is genuinely awkward.

blocks.title: When you're asked how it's been and you honestly can't say
blocks.body: "Up and down" is the truest answer most people can give after six months. A fortnight of small daily notes turns that into something a nurse can actually work with.

blocks.title: When it keeps happening in the same place
blocks.body: The cold walk to the bus. Hoovering the back room. One particular hill. Naming the exposure is the part you can do something about.

blocks.title: When you're reaching for the reliever more than you used to
blocks.body: SteadyAir counts it and tells you when the count has moved. Then it points you at a person. It does not tell you to take anything, and it never will.

blocks.title: When you want the clinic to see it
blocks.body: One tidy page of your own notes, previewed by you, sent by you, whenever you decide. Never automatically.

blocks.title: What it isn't
blocks.body: It doesn't measure anything — no spirometry, no oxygen readings, nothing paired to your phone. It doesn't name a medicine or a dose. It doesn't decide whether you're having a flare-up. And it is not a way to get hold of someone quickly in an emergency.

S02.footer: Education and self-management support. Not a diagnosis or treatment.

S03.title: Consent & privacy
S03.headline: What we hold, and what we don't.

blocks.title: Held on your phone
blocks.body: Your daily ratings, your reliever counts, your trigger list and anything you type. These stay here unless you send them.

blocks.title: Shared with your clinic
blocks.body: Nothing, by default. When you do send something, it is the summary you looked at and approved — never a live feed, and never an alert we raise on your behalf.

blocks.title: You can leave
blocks.body: Export the lot as a readable file, or delete it. Deletion is completed on your phone and on our servers, not hidden from view.

blocks.title: One thing to be clear about
blocks.body: Nobody is watching this. If your numbers move, SteadyAir tells you — it does not tell your clinic, and no one is going to call you because of something you typed here.

items.title: Let SteadyAir remind me when a summary is worth sending
items.body: Reminders only. It still doesn't send anything by itself.

S03.footer: You can change either choice later in Settings.

S04.title: Your first fortnight
S04.headline: Change nothing for two weeks.
S04.sub: Carry on exactly as you were. Without a starting picture, neither of us can tell later whether anything you tried made a difference.

blocks.title: Your two hardest mornings
blocks.body: Thursday and Saturday, both under freezing, both days you walked to the bus. That's the only thing SteadyAir has spotted so far, and it may well be a coincidence.

blocks.title: You don't have to wait out the fortnight
blocks.body: If you'd rather get on with it, do. We'll mark the starting picture as partial and say so on every chart that uses it.

actions.label: Skip the rest of the fortnight

S04.footer: These are your own ratings, in your own words. SteadyAir has not measured anything and does not treat them as measurements.

S05.title: What sets it off
S05.headline: When does your chest get worse?
S05.sub: Tick what's true. Your fortnight already suggests a couple, so those start ticked — untick anything that's wrong, because your account beats our guess.

How it starts
blocks.body: Same words we'll offer you at check-in, so they'll look familiar later.

blocks.title: Cold mornings, four times out of five.
blocks.body: Your four hardest days were all under freezing and all began with the walk to the bus stop. That is why Cold air and Hills or stairs are already ticked.

blocks.title: If smoking is on this list
blocks.body: Your own, or somebody else's in the house. Stopping is the single biggest thing available here, and it has a whole programme of its own — BreatheFree. SteadyAir isn't going to do a worse version of it. Joining that one changes nothing here, and the two keep separate records.
None of this is fixed. Every check-in nudges this list, and what SteadyAir suggests moves with it.

S05.footer: Kept on your phone. Not shared with anyone.

S06.title: What you'll try
S06.headline: Pick what you'll actually do.
S06.sub: Two small things beat five good intentions. You can change any of it later, and nothing here is graded.

blocks.title: Days a week you'll check in
blocks.body: Five is plenty. Seven is not better, and missing one is not a failure.

items.title: Cover your mouth and nose on cold mornings
items.body: A scarf on the walk to the bus. Cold air was in four of your five hardest days.

items.title: Open the window before you hoover, and go slower
items.body: The back room came up twice in your fortnight.

items.title: Ask about pulmonary rehab at your next appointment
items.body: Not something SteadyAir can arrange or judge you on. It's a question to take in, and it sits on your appointment list until you tick it off.

blocks.title: When we'll nudge you
blocks.body: One reminder, and it says nothing on your lock screen beyond the word SteadyAir.

blocks.title: Nothing on this screen is a medical target
blocks.body: SteadyAir does not set a dose, a distance, a number of steps or a number of puffs. It has no view on any of those. Everything above is a change to what you meet in a day, chosen by you.

S06.footer: You can edit any of this from Settings, at any time, without explaining why.

S07.title: Review your plan
S07.headline: That's the whole thing.
S07.sub: It is deliberately small. Have a look, then start it.

blocks.title: Light touch — one check-in and a running count
blocks.body: No blocking, no scoring, no streak. If it ever starts feeling like homework, turn the reminder off and keep the log.

blocks.title: What starting actually switches on
blocks.body: An evening reminder and the reliever count. That's it. Nothing is shared, nobody is notified, and your fortnight of notes is kept.

blocks.body: If your reliever count climbs, we'll say so and point you at Nurse Pike the same day. It is the only unprompted thing this app does.

S09.title: Daily check-in
S09.headline: How's the chest been today?
S09.sub: No right answers, and no wrong ones. A rough guess is worth far more than a skipped day.

blocks.title: Overall, today
Worst your breathing got
blocks.body: Ten is fighting for every breath. Zero is not noticing it at all.

blocks.title: How many times did you reach for your reliever?
blocks.body: Your best guess. We count it, we don't grade it.

blocks.title: Anything else today?
If it's bad while you're reading this
blocks.body: Struggling to get the words out, lips or fingertips gone dusky, or frightened by it — stop filling this in and call 911. A check-in is not the thing that helps in that minute.

S09.footer: This is how you felt, in your words. SteadyAir has measured nothing and does not treat these as clinical readings.

S10.title: Your readings
S10.headline: What you've written down.
S10.sub: Two numbers a day and the dates they happened on. That's all this page is.

blocks.title: If you are fighting for breath, call 911 now.
blocks.body: Can't finish a sentence, lips or fingertips gone dusky, chest pain with it, or suddenly much worse than you have ever been — that is an emergency, and it is not something to log first. Logging can wait. It always can.

blocks.eyebrow: Not an emergency, but not for next month either
blocks.title: Your reliever count has gone up three days running.
blocks.body: Eleven this week against four the week before. SteadyAir is not telling you what that means and is not going to — but a change of that shape is exactly what Nurse Pike asks people to come in about, and she has same-day slots for it. Ring Elm Road today rather than waiting for 3 March.

blocks.title: Reliever, today
Breathing, today
There is no good number on this page
blocks.body: SteadyAir does not score these, does not colour them, and has no threshold it is quietly comparing you against. A six is not worse than a four in any sense the app understands — it is a different day, and only you know what was going on in it. What the pattern means belongs to Nurse Pike.

blocks.title: Why the count matters more than the rating
blocks.body: How breathless you felt is yours. How often you reached for the reliever is the bit clinics tend to act on, which is why that is the number SteadyAir watches for movement — and the only thing it ever does about it is tell you, and give you the phone number.

S10.footer: Your own counts, typed by you. Nothing here was measured, and nothing here has been sent to anyone.

blocks.title: Smoking has its own programme
blocks.body: There is no short version of it worth reading, so SteadyAir doesn't write one. BreatheFree does that job properly, keeps its own separate record, and does not touch anything in here.

blocks.title: What this library will not do
blocks.body: These explain. They don't prescribe. Nothing here names a medicine, a strength, a dose, or when to reach for one — that belongs to whoever prescribed it, and they know things about you that an app never will.

blocks.title: Why the dates are on the front
blocks.body: Anything not checked in eighteen months comes down rather than sitting here looking current.

S11.footer: Reviewed before it goes up, and dated so you can see how old it is.

S12.title: Progress
S12.headline: Six weeks, honestly drawn.
S12.sub: Including the bits that went badly, which are the bits worth showing someone.

blocks.title: The two numbers are not moving together
blocks.body: Your ratings this week are close to where they started — 4.4 against 4.6. Your reliever count nearly tripled. That is the whole reason SteadyAir watches the count rather than the rating, and it is the pair of numbers worth putting in front of Nurse Pike.

blocks.title: It's the cold, and it's the mornings.
blocks.body: Four of your five hardest days this month began with the walk to the bus, and every one of them was under freezing. Weeks 3 and 4, when it was milder, were your two easiest — the scarf started in week 4, so we can't tell those two apart yet.

blocks.title: March is still in these charts.
blocks.body: The five weeks after that chest infection were your worst, and they are in every average on this page. A bad stretch isn't a slip and it isn't a failure — nobody chooses a chest infection. SteadyAir keeps it as history because a chart that quietly drops your worst month is no use to Nurse Pike and no comfort to you.

blocks.title: Delete everything
blocks.body: Completed, not hidden — your phone, our servers, and anything queued to sync. It cannot be undone and it ends this programme.
